questions.title: Service Discovery with Eureka
questions.question: How does service discovery work in Spring Cloud using Eureka?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Service registry: central catalog of service instances and their addresses**
- **Eureka server: registry; Eureka client: each service registers on startup**
- **Client-side load balancing: Spring Cloud LoadBalancer picks instance from registry**
- **Heartbeat: clients send heartbeats; registry evicts dead instances**
- **`@LoadBalanced` + service name in URL: `http://ORDER-SERVICE/api/orders`**
- **Alternative: Consul, Kubernetes native discovery (preferred in K8s environments)**

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Service discovery solves the problem of dynamic service addresses. In a containerized environment, services spin up and down with different IPs and ports. Rather than hardcoding addresses, each service registers itself with a central registry (Eureka Server) including its host, port, and health status.

When Service A needs to call Service B, instead of using a hardcoded URL, it asks the registry for instances of 'ORDER-SERVICE', gets back a list, and picks one (client-side load balancing). Spring Cloud makes this transparent: you just annotate your RestTemplate or WebClient with `@LoadBalanced` and use the service name as the hostname.

In Kubernetes, you'd typically use Kubernetes native service discovery (DNS-based, via Services and kube-dns) rather than Eureka, since K8s already provides this functionality built-in.
